title: Ignition Temperature
description: Why does a matchstick light but a lump of coal needs more heat? Master ignition temperature to grab ember 3.

content.value: A fuel will not burn until it is hot enough. The lowest temperature at which a substance catches fire and starts to burn is called its IGNITION TEMPERATURE. Below this temperature, no matter how much fuel and oxygen you have, it will not ignite.

Different substances have different ignition temperatures. Paper and a matchstick have a LOW ignition temperature, so they catch fire easily. Coal has a HIGH ignition temperature, so it needs a lot of heating before it starts to burn.

LOW ignition temperature  → catches fire easily  📄 paper, 🔥 matchstick
HIGH ignition temperature → needs lots of heat    🪨 coal, 🪵 thick wood

When you strike a matchstick, the friction produces just enough heat to reach the ignition temperature of the chemicals on its tip — so it bursts into flame. This is why we usually need a spark or flame to START a fire: to supply that initial heat.
You cannot make a fuel burn below its ignition temperature. That's exactly why cooling a fire with water works — water lowers the temperature below ignition point.

Key Takeaway: The ignition temperature is the lowest temperature at which a substance catches fire. Fuels with a low ignition temperature (paper, matches) light easily; those with a high one (coal) need much more heat.

quiz.question: The ignition temperature of a substance is…
options: the lowest temperature at which it catches fire
the temperature at which it melts
quiz.explain: Ignition temperature is the lowest temperature at which a fuel catches fire and burns.

quiz.question: Paper catches fire more easily than coal because paper has a…
quiz.explain: Paper's low ignition temperature means it needs less heat to start burning than coal.

quiz.question: A fuel below its ignition temperature will…
options: not catch fire, even with fuel and oxygen present
quiz.explain: Without reaching the ignition temperature, a fuel cannot catch fire — this is why cooling puts out fire.
